SALARY RANGE POSTING CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your job posting state a pay range?

Paste the posting text and pick the state(s) it could be filled from. Get an instant read on whether the wording states a dollar range, and which of those states currently require one by law — with the law, effective date, and size threshold cited.

Nothing you paste is uploaded — this scans your text and looks up a fixed reference table entirely in this browser. Not legal advice. See the disclaimer below before you rely on this.

1. Scan a posting against selected states

Ctrl/Cmd-click to select more than one — useful for a remote posting open to several states.

Prefer a CLI, or want this in a script?

Same table and scan, zero dependencies, one file:

node cli.mjs scan "$60,000 - $80,000 per year" --states CO,NY
node cli.mjs scan --file posting.txt --states California,Texas --json
node cli.mjs states

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call ever. scan exits 1 when a selected state requires a range and none was detected, so it doubles as a one-line reminder in a posting-review checklist or CI step for an ATS template.

All 14 jurisdictions with a posting-range law, and the other 37 + DC without one

Covers only the requirement to state a range IN the posting itself — not a different-point-in-process rule (Connecticut, Nevada, Rhode Island, and others), and not city/county ordinances layered on top. Full scope and caveats: why this varies by state.

StateRequires range?LawEffectiveThreshold

Common questions

Which US states currently require a pay range in the job posting itself?

As of this tool's last check (September 2026): Colorado, California, Washington, New York, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Vermont, the District of Columbia, Massachusetts, Virginia, and Maine. Each has its own effective date and employer-size threshold, shown in the table below. Several other states and cities require disclosure at a different point in the process (upon request, before an interview, after an offer) rather than in the ad — this tool does not cover those.

How does this tool decide whether my posting text has a range?

It is a literal text scan: it looks for two dollar figures close together, joined by a dash, en dash, or the word "to" or "through" (like "$60,000 - $80,000" or "$28.50 to $34.00 per hour"). It does not understand whether the number is a good-faith range, a wage versus a bonus figure, or whether your specific posting is otherwise compliant — it only reports what the wording contains.

Is this legal advice, or a guarantee my posting is compliant?

No. This is a text-pattern scan plus a reference lookup against a fixed table of state posting-range laws, current as of the date shown. It does not know your employer's size, whether the role is exempt, or your specific state's current statute text, and it does not cover city or county ordinances layered on top of state law. Verify against your state's labor agency or an employment attorney before relying on this.

Is anything I type uploaded anywhere?

No. The posting text you paste and the states you pick are scanned and looked up entirely in your browser from a fixed table shipped with the page. Nothing is sent anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either. The "Copy shareable link" button carries only your selected states into the link — never the posting text.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal advice, and it does not replace a qualified employment attorney. It reports a literal text-pattern scan of the words you pasted and a fixed table's state-level posting-range classification — nothing more — and it does not know your employer's size, industry-specific exemptions, or whether a city/county ordinance also applies. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including checking your state's current guidance. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (posting_scanned, example_loaded, link_shared, link_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. The "Copy shareable link" button puts only your selected states into the link itself — the posting text never leaves this page. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: Call Recording Consent Check covers a different US-state-law reference problem (recording a phone call, not posting a job) in the same style. If you're comparing this to just checking each state's law by hand, see how this compares to a manual lookup.

Employing people in the EU? EU Pay Gap Report Calculator computes the pay transparency reporting indicators the Directive requires, from a payroll table you paste.

Free and open source. If this saved you a compliance headache, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-each-states-law-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. checking each state's law by hand

The usual way to answer "does my posting need a salary range?" is to search "does [state] require a salary range in job postings," read whichever page ranks first, and eyeball your own draft against it. That answers the legal question well enough most of the time. It does not scan the posting you actually wrote, and it does not scale past one or two states.

What each one is for

A one-off search is free and needs no tool: type the state name, read the first confident-sounding answer. It works fine for a single-state posting and a careful reader.

This checker scans the exact text you drafted for a stated range, checks it against every state the role could be filled from in one pass, and names the specific law, effective date, and threshold for each state that requires one — from one paste rather than several searches and a manual re-read.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Does Colorado require a posted pay range?Either one. A single search answers this, and so does this checker's table.
Does the posting I already wrote actually have a range in it?This checker. A search engine has never seen your draft; it can only tell you the rule, not whether your wording satisfies it.
A remote posting is open to candidates in six states — which ones need a range?This checker, in one pass. Six separate searches plus a manual cross-check against one draft is the same task done the slow way.
Is anything I paste uploaded anywhere?Neither. A search involves no tool of ours at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Isn't searching "does [state] require a salary range in job postings" enough?

It answers the single-state legal question, and plenty of free pages already answer it correctly. What it does not do is look at your actual posting text and tell you whether it already has a range in the shape the law expects — that is a second, separate step a search result cannot do for you.

What does a one-off search not give you that this tool does?

Two things bundled together: a scan of the exact wording you already drafted (does it read as a range, a single figure, or nothing), and the requirement for every state the role could be filled from checked in one pass — rather than one search per state and a manual re-read of your draft against each answer.

Why does this matter more for a remote or multi-state posting?

A single-state posting only needs one search. A remote posting open to candidates in ten states needs ten separate lookups done correctly and then cross-referenced against one draft by hand — exactly the kind of repetitive check that is easy to get half-right under deadline pressure, and easy to re-run here in one pass.

Does this replace reading the actual law that applies to you?

No, and it says so on every page. It names the public law for each state so the next step is reading that law's current text or your state labor agency's guidance, not a general search that may surface an outdated summary.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. They are not legal advice, and they do not replace a qualified employment attorney. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Checking each state's law by hand" describes a manual habit anyone can do with a search engine, not any company's product or service.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere.

why-pay-range-laws-differ-by-state.html.text:
← back to the checker

Why pay-range posting laws differ by state

"Does my state require a salary range in job postings?" has a different answer depending on exactly what you mean by "require" and "in job postings" — this page is the scope this tool actually checks, and the parts it deliberately leaves for you to verify.

What "requires a range" means here

Fourteen states and DC currently require the job posting or advertisement itself to state a good-faith pay range: Colorado, California, Washington, New York, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Vermont, the District of Columbia, Massachusetts, Virginia, and Maine. Each has its own effective date and, in most cases, an employer-size threshold below which the law does not apply — both shown in the table on the checker page.

What is deliberately not modeled

  • Disclose-at-a-different-point laws. Connecticut, Nevada, Rhode Island, and a few others require disclosure when a candidate asks, before an interview, or after an offer — not in the ad itself. Reporting these as "not required" for a posting-scan question would misread the actual rule; they are out of scope rather than answered incorrectly.
  • City and county ordinances. Cincinnati, Toledo, Columbus, Jersey City, and others run their own local posting rules independent of state law, sometimes with a different threshold. A posting can pass every state-level check here and still need a separate local check.
  • Exemptions and edge cases. Some states exempt commission-only roles, certain government positions, or internal transfers. This table does not encode those carve-outs.
  • Whether your employer actually meets the threshold. The table states each threshold this build is confident of; it has no way to know your employer's actual headcount or where your employees are.

What the text scan actually checks

The scan looks for two dollar amounts close together in your pasted text, joined by a dash, en dash, or the word "to" or "through" — the shape of "$60,000 - $80,000" or "$28.50 to $34.00 per hour." That is a literal pattern match, not an understanding of the sentence. It cannot tell a good-faith range from two unrelated figures that happen to land near each other, and it has no idea whether the number it found is a base wage, a bonus target, or a total-comp estimate. Read the sentence yourself before trusting the classification for anything that matters.

How this can be wrong

Three ways, in order of how often they matter: (1) the scan misreads adjacent-but-unrelated figures as a range, or reads a genuine range as unrelated figures, because it has no understanding of sentence structure; (2) a threshold or effective date drifts after this table was last checked — state legislatures amend these rules most heavily at the start of each year; (3) a jurisdiction adds or repeals a posting-range requirement entirely and this table has not yet been updated to reflect it. None of these is caught automatically — verify against your state's labor agency or current counsel before relying on a specific posting decision.

Common questions

Why do some states require a range "upon request" instead of in the posting?

Connecticut, Nevada, Rhode Island, and a few others were early movers that required disclosure at a different point — when a candidate asks, before the first interview, or after an offer is made — rather than baking it into the ad itself. Those laws answer a related but different question than "does this posting have a range," so this tool's posting-text scan deliberately does not check them: reporting "not required" for a rule that fires later in the process would be a false negative on the actual question those states ask.

Does this cover city or county ordinances?

No. Several cities and counties — Cincinnati, Toledo, Columbus, and Jersey City among them — run their own posting ordinances independent of their state's law, sometimes with a different threshold or scope. A posting can clear every state-level check this tool runs and still need a separate local check this tool does not do.

How was the effective-date and threshold data checked?

Cross-checked against multiple current employment-law-firm and HR-vendor summaries at build time (September 2026), not against a single source or a pinpoint statute citation. Entries marked with a lower-confidence threshold say so explicitly rather than asserting a number this build is not sure of.

What does the posting-text scan actually look for?

Two dollar amounts close together in the text, joined by a dash, en dash, or the word "to" or "through." It has no idea whether that number is a good-faith range as the statute defines it, a base wage versus a signing bonus, or whether the role is exempt from the law entirely — it is a literal pattern match on the wording, nothing more.

They are not legal advice, and they do not replace a qualified employment attorney. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.
